doc.title: Iola Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Wilton, CT, July 17, 2011

title: Early quartet touring, pay and splitting the take
summary: Touring in a station wagon, low pay despite the 1954 Time cover, $1,000 a night contracts, and Dave's pay agreement with Paul.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: Yeah. Well with the quartet, with the addition of Paul, was the beginning of actual touring outside of San Francisco, Los Angeles, Portland, Salt Lake, that was kind of what they did. And those were tough days too because the pay wasn’t that great. Four guys in a station wagon, along with the instruments and, again, it had to be a great commitment on everybody’s part. So it really wasn’t — see the Time magazine cover was in 1954. And one would assume that was sort of, you know, at the height. And actually it wasn’t. I mean the pay was still low and the touring was still tough. It was a period where you began to see a brighter future but it wasn’t a big payoff.
Well can you recall what the quartet would have got for one average gig? How much money they would have made?

Well this much I can remember. Going to the bank in Oakland when we were proposing to build a house on a lot that had been given to Dave when he got out of the Army. We didn’t have the money that we needed in order to get a loan, but we had some contracts for the future. And the contracts for the future for the quartet was $1,000 a night for the quartet, and that was the highest we had ever received at that point. Well realize that out of this $1,000, we pay a commission, transportation to get there, you pay the guys, you pay Social Security, unemployment insurance, liability, and you’re not left with that much.
And did he pay the other three guys before he paid himself?

He and Paul had an agreement. The rhythm section would be guaranteed a salary. And the agreement with Paul was — I don’t remember the exact amount, whether it was 40 percent or 50 percent or what it was, whatever the gross was, I’ve forgotten just what the percentage was. So sometimes it ended up that Dave ended up with very little. Because he was paying the transportation, the commissions, and that sort of thing.
